objective: Audit whether SERENIoT's cross-device whitelist-generalization gap supports a low-cost, falsifiable test with matched device families and separate false-allow and false-block endpoints.

decision.basis: The endpoint gap is testable with a small number of matched physical devices and packet traces, but the original SERENIoT implementation/data and the follow-up IoT Inspector data are not presently public in a directly runnable form. A positive deployment or functionality result must not be interpreted as a security benefit.

sources_and_data.title: SERENIoT: Collaborative Network Security Policy Management and Enforcement for Smart Homes
observations: The open problem is determining the correct network behavior to whitelist.
A packet signature is H(protocol, endpoint, service port); endpoint is a domain name or IP when a domain is unavailable.
Device types are grouped by the sorted set of packet signatures, without device-specific identifiers.
The whitelist contains signatures observed by the majority of Sentinels for the device type; every packet not specified in the whitelist is discarded.
The threat model concerns changed outbound or inbound behavior, while local-network traffic and malicious use of valid credentials are out of scope.
The evaluation used simulated Sentinels plus three LIFX Mini bulbs, and demonstrated convergence/performance, not matched false-allow and false-block rates.

sources_and_data.title: Making Interactions With Home IoT Devices More Secure, Private, and Usable
sources_and_data.author: Pranshu Chatterjee
sources_and_data.public_date_bound: 2022-07-07 mailing-list attachment date; exact dissertation deposit date not independently authenticated
observations: The follow-up explicitly says SERENIoT does not study generalizing traffic data or how policies generalize across devices, and flags load balancing as an outside-lab concern.
Its own experiment generates allowlists from IoT Inspector traffic and applies them to disjoint held-out devices; D and D' are required to be disjoint.
Its policy family is not SERENIoT's native majority packet-signature rule: it varies hostname, domain, pattern, IP and thresholds requiring a host to appear on n devices.
Its main retrospective endpoint, MFAF, is the median fraction of observed flows allowed; this is a legitimate-flow-coverage measure, not a false-allow rate.
The lab study tested nine products and 52 functionalities; observed failures were functionality blocking, not a controlled estimate of malicious traffic accepted.

sources_and_data.title: IoT Inspector: Crowdsourcing Labeled Network Traffic from Smart Home Devices at Scale
observations: The follow-up reports 5,439 validated devices, 424 products, 80 vendors, 43 device types, 1,468 households and 38,164,870 flows collected from 2019-04-08 through 2019-07-24 in the analyzed subset.
The follow-up states that the full IoT Inspector dataset cannot be shared without original-author IRB permission; it supplies synthetic sample data instead.
Public IoT Inspector software is accessible, but that does not provide the historical labeled flow corpus or the follow-up's processed subset.

The follow-up claims its analysis and firewall code were available in an anonymized GitHub repository cited only as reference [228] in the inspected dissertation; the dissertation reference gives no resolvable repository URL. The original SERENIoT paper likewise did not expose a verified runnable artifact URL in the inspected text.
Therefore public-data replay and exact artifact replication were not feasible from the inspected public materials alone.

original_sereniot_policy.device_grouping: same sorted signature set; no device-specific identifier
original_sereniot_policy.admission: signature observed by the majority of Sentinels for the device type
original_sereniot_policy.update_rule: behavior changes are incorporated when majority observations support them

follow_up_policy.admission: host appears in at least n distinct training devices for the selected product/sample
follow_up_policy.enforcement: traffic not matching the selected representation is blocked; DNS resolution and cold-start behavior affect enforcement
follow_up_policy.evaluation_split: training devices and held-out devices are disjoint

policy_reconciliation.reconciliation: Both are default-deny allowlisting from observed network behavior and both target transfer across distinct devices, but they are not the same intervention. The follow-up is endpoint-relevant scope-narrowing evidence, not a direct SERENIoT replication or resolution.

false_block.definition: A ground-truth legitimate flow or required user-visible device function is rejected by the frozen whitelist.
false_block.primary_measure: per-flow false-block rate on held-out benign/update traces, plus per-functionality failure rate in a blinded functionality checklist
false_block.related_follow_up_measure: MFAF = median fraction of held-out observed flows allowed; report 1-MFAF only as a coverage-derived proxy, not as a complete false-block label
false_block.required_ground_truth: independently frozen legitimate-flow/functionality labels and a predeclared handling rule for previously unseen but legitimate endpoints

false_allow.definition: A flow independently labeled unauthorized or attacker-injected is accepted by the frozen whitelist.
false_allow.primary_measure: per-flow false-allow rate on seeded attack traces, reported separately by attack family and host representation
false_allow.related_follow_up_measure: attack-surface breadth is only a proxy; the follow-up's domain/pattern discussion does not establish a false-allow rate
false_allow.required_ground_truth: a separate attack trace set with known unauthorized destinations/ports and no contamination of whitelist-construction traces

endpoints.non_equivalence_warning: Do not combine false-allow and false-block into one accuracy score, and do not call MFAF, functionality success, convergence, or throughput a security outcome.

feasible_test.hypothesis: Under a frozen SERENIoT packet-signature policy, a whitelist learned from one or more devices in a matched product family transfers to held-out physical devices with lower false-block than a single-device whitelist, without increasing false-allow beyond a predeclared margin.
competing_explanations: Observed transfer is caused by shared vendor endpoints or common firmware rather than collaborative majority learning.
Endpoint churn, regional routing, load balancing, DNS resolution or software updates cause false blocks independent of device-family similarity.
A permissive domain/pattern abstraction reduces false blocks but increases false allows; apparent improvement is a policy-representation trade-off, not generalization.

low_cost_design.units: At least two matched device families, with at least 3 physical devices per family when available; separate training and held-out devices and, if possible, separate homes/networks.
arms: native SERENIoT signature whitelist learned from one training device
native SERENIoT signature whitelist learned by majority/union rule from the remaining training devices
follow-up-style hostname/pattern or domain comparator, labeled as a different policy rather than SERENIoT
low_cost_design.split: No device may contribute to both whitelist construction and held-out evaluation; freeze signatures/thresholds before opening held-out traces.
low_cost_design.analysis: Report per-family and pooled counts with exact denominators, confidence intervals clustered by physical device, and separate false-block and false-allow tables.

feasible_test.falsification_gate: The proposed generalization claim fails if the majority-trained policy does not reduce held-out false blocks relative to the single-device policy, or if its false-allow rate exceeds the predeclared margin; either endpoint may independently falsify the claim.

observed: The source and follow-up endpoint definitions are reconciled and materially differ in policy construction.
The follow-up supplies a device-disjoint split concept and demonstrates that cross-device transfer is measurable, but its reported results do not provide SERENIoT false-allow/false-block estimates.
A low-cost matched-device test is conceptually feasible with packet capture and a small lab, provided legitimate and attack labels are frozen independently.
blockers: The IoT Inspector historical corpus is not publicly downloadable from the inspected sources and requires permission/IRB access.
The follow-up's anonymized analysis/firewall repository was not resolvable from the cited dissertation text, and a verified SERENIoT runnable artifact was not found in the inspected original paper.
No matched physical-device traces, ground-truth attack traces, or current endpoint labels were available in this workspace, so no experiment was executed.
observed_result_or_blocker.negative_result_preserved: No direct evidence was found that SERENIoT's native policy achieves safe cross-device generalization; no direct evidence was found that it fails. Search/access failure is not treated as a negative scientific result.

uncertainty: The follow-up is a public dissertation with a dated mailing-list attachment, not an independently verified replication of SERENIoT.
MFAF captures allowed observed traffic and cannot identify malicious traffic accepted by an allowlist.
The exact source implementation, chain state, reverse-DNS behavior and majority timing may affect reproducibility beyond the paper's policy description.
A small lab sample can test the frozen endpoint mechanics but cannot establish deployment-wide security or prevalence.
next_falsifiable_action: Acquire authorized current packet traces or collect a preregistered small matched-device dataset; implement the exact SERENIoT signature rule H(protocol, endpoint, service_port), freeze device-disjoint training/held-out splits and policy update timing, seed independently labeled unauthorized destinations, and report false-block and false-allow endpoints separately before considering any broader claim.
